title: Estimating Probabilities Using Simulation
rights: Original teacher-authored public-safe practice; no secure assessments.

items.prompt: When one complete trial is three independent fair coin tosses, which is one possible outcome of that trial?
items.hint: Distinguish a complete trial from one toss within it.
items.solution: An outcome records the result of one complete three-toss trial. The sequence HTH is one of eight ordered outcomes.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe practice, November 2026

options.label: A
options.text: A three-letter ordered sequence, such as HTH

options.label: B
options.text: An individual result H only

options.label: C
options.text: The proportion of heads among 100 tosses

options.label: D
options.text: Exactly one head, with no order recorded

items.prompt: A simulation of 600 complete four-spin trials recorded at least one prize in 417 groups. What is the estimated probability of that event?
items.hint: Match the denominator to the unit counted in the numerator.
items.solution: The event is success of the entire four-spin group. The estimate is 417/600=0.695, not 417/2400.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe practice, November 2026

items.prompt: An independent fair coin has landed heads seven times in succession. What is the probability that the next toss is tails?
items.hint: Does the coin remember prior results?
items.solution: Independence means the next toss is unaffected by the previous seven. P(Tails)=1/2. The law of large numbers does not force compensation.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe practice, November 2026

options.label: D
options.text: Greater than 1/2

items.prompt: A population process has a 30% success probability. Which mapping of ten equally likely digits is valid?
items.hint: How many of ten digits equal 30%?
items.solution: Exactly three of the ten equally likely digits must signal success, so digits 0, 1 and 2 yield 3/10=0.30.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe practice, November 2026

options.label: A
options.text: Use digits 0–2 for success and 3–9 for failure

options.label: B
options.text: Use digits 0–3 for success and 4–9 for failure

options.label: C
options.text: Use even digits for success and odd digits for failure

options.label: D
options.text: Use digit 0 for success and all other digits for failure

items.prompt: A student simulates 250 trials of two fair dice and counts 37 pairs with sum at least 10. Which calculation estimates the probability of that event?
items.hint: A pair of rolls constitutes one trial.
items.solution: Each trial consists of a pair of rolls. The 37 successful pairs out of 250 complete pairs give 37/250=0.148.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe practice, November 2026

items.prompt: Which statement about a larger correctly designed simulation is most accurate?
items.hint: Consider whether the law is monotonic.
items.solution: The law of large numbers is a long-run tendency, not a step-by-step guarantee. More repetitions reduce random variation but cannot correct a wrong model.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe practice, November 2026

options.label: A
options.text: Its estimated probability must become closer to the true value after every new trial

options.label: B
options.text: After 1,000 trials, its estimate must equal the model probability exactly

options.label: C
options.text: A larger number of trials can repair a simulator that uses the wrong success probability

options.label: D
options.text: Its relative frequency generally stabilizes toward the model probability, but can temporarily move away

items.prompt: A student makes codes 00 through 20 inclusive represent a 20% chance using uniform two-digit numbers 00–99. What is wrong?
items.solution: Count the codes inclusively: 00, 01, ..., 20 are 21 of the 100 possible codes, giving 0.21. To model 20%, use 00–19.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe practice, November 2026

options.label: A
options.text: It represents 19%, because 00 is not a number

options.label: B
options.text: It represents 21%, because 00 through 20 contains 21 equally likely codes

options.label: C
options.text: It represents exactly 20%

options.label: D
options.text: It represents 2%, because only 00 and 20 count

items.prompt: Which interpretation properly separates simulation from theoretical probability?
items.hint: A model probability and an estimate answer related but distinct questions.
items.solution: The estimate 505/1000=0.505 varies randomly around the theoretical P=0.5; no finite run is guaranteed to match exactly.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe practice, November 2026

options.label: A
options.text: A recorded estimate 0.505 proves the true chance is 0.505

options.label: B
options.text: A simulated 505 successes out of 1,000 trials can estimate a theoretical chance of 0.5 without contradicting it

options.label: C
options.text: A probability of 0.5 guarantees exactly 500 successes in the next 1,000 trials

options.label: D
options.text: Simulation results can be treated as unbiased even when the random device has the wrong probabilities
